about.title: Fairfield Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall rarely feels like a legal matter in the moment. You are on the ground in a grocery aisle off North Texas Street, or in a parking lot along Travis Boulevard, and the first thoughts are about pain and embarrassment, not paperwork. Yet under California premises liability law, what happens in the next few hours matters. The injured person generally has to show the property owner knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have, and did nothing to fix it or warn about it. That is called notice, and it is where many Fairfield fall claims turn. Photos of the spill, the broken step, or the missing handrail, taken before anything is cleaned up, carry real weight. So does surveillance footage, which many Solano County businesses overwrite within days. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Fairfield residents with an independent attorney who handles these cases on contingency, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Fairfield Residents Turn to LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Attorneys who understand the notice requirement
items.desc: California asks fall victims to prove the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The attorneys in our network build that proof through inspection records, incident reports, and witness accounts rather than relying on the injury alone.

items.title: Fast action on surveillance video and evidence
items.desc: Most stores and apartment complexes in Solano County keep camera footage only briefly. An attorney can send a preservation demand quickly so the recording of your fall is not erased before anyone reviews it.

items.title: Deadlines and shared fault handled correctly
items.desc: You generally have two years to file, but a fall on city or county property triggers a much shorter government claim window. California also uses pure comparative fault, so being partly to blame reduces a claim rather than ending it, and an attorney can push back on inflated blame.

items.question: I tripped on a broken sidewalk in Fairfield. Is the city responsible?
items.answer: Possibly, but the rules are different when a public entity like the City of Fairfield or Solano County owns the property. You typically must file a formal government claim within six months of the injury, far sooner than the two-year deadline that applies to private owners. You also need to show the entity had notice of the defect and a reasonable chance to repair it. Because that window closes quickly, it helps to speak with an attorney early.

items.question: The store manager told me I should have been watching where I was walking. Does that end my case?
items.answer: No. California follows pure comparative fault, which means a claim can proceed even if you share some responsibility. If a jury or insurer decides you were partly at fault, your compensation is reduced by that percentage rather than eliminated. An attorney can gather evidence showing the hazard was not reasonably visible or that no warning was posted.

items.question: What should I do in the first few days after a fall on someone else's property?
items.answer: Get medical care first, and ask for records of your visit. Photograph the exact spot where you fell, including any liquid, debris, lighting, or missing signage, and write down the names of anyone who saw it happen. Ask the business for a copy of any incident report and request in writing that they preserve surveillance footage. Then reach out to LawProactive so an attorney can take over the evidence work while you focus on healing.
